facts.fcStory: Where the k = 6 run left the plain run, the candidates were tied to within bfloat16 rounding, and different ways of computing the same position disagreed on the winner: on the summarize prompt at token 3 (after "Large language"), the plain run chose " models", the k = 6 run " model", and recomputing that position as one full pass, one token at a time and in blocks of 7 gave " model", " model" and " model", with the top two logits 0.000, 0.250 and 0.250 apart; on the story prompt at token 51 (after "rifted from the sea, its"), the plain run chose " cap", the k = 6 run " label", and recomputing that position as one full pass, one token at a time and in blocks of 7 gave " surface", " surface" and " surface", with the top two logits 0.125, 0.000 and 0.125 apart.
facts.treeVerdict: By prompt (chain of 8 against tree of 8): code edit 3.69 against 3.62; summary 1.69 against 2.10; story 0.89 against 1.39; list 7.42 against 5.75. The tree wins where the draft is unsure (summary, story), because its second and third guesses near the root often hold the target's choice; it loses on the list, where the draft's single chain is almost always right and the tree, capped here at depth 6 and spending nodes on alternatives, cannot reach as deep.
facts.xLoad: One-minute load average before each run: 5.0 to 26.8 (median 7.0) on 10 cores; other agents shared the machine.
facts.xNote: llama-server, Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M target and Qwen3-0.6B Q4_K_M draft, one 16-slot server per configuration with B concurrent clients, greedy, mixed prompts, 192 tokens per answer; bars are the lowest and highest ratios over the two sweeps. Synthetic acceptance (llama-server's --spec-synth-len) runs the real draft but fixes the mean acceptance length, so it isolates cost from guess quality.
facts.xSummary: on this laptop the 0.6B draft never paid: 0.70x the plain server's throughput at 1 user, 0.54x at 16. Even with an artificially excellent drafter (acceptance length 4.5) the best was 1.16x (at 8 users), and 0.89x at 16.
facts.xText: On the laptop the real 0.6B draft (k = 3, measured acceptance length 2.48 on this prompt mix) gave 0.70x the plain server's throughput at 1 user, 0.67x at 4 and 0.54x at 16 users. With llama-server's synthetic acceptance fixing the acceptance length at 4.5, better than any drafter here, the ratio was 0.95x at 1 user, at best 1.16x (8 users) and 0.89x at 16 measured here. This laptop is past the crossover from the first user: checking 4 guesses costs 2.68x a one-token step (section 1), so even 4.5 tokens per step barely repays the drafting. On an H100, where the check is nearly free, the same acceptance length would give a large gain at small batch (the cost model's H100 setting, below).
facts.m1Story: the model predicts 0.52x at one user, a slow-down.

sd-pr1.text: Measured: 2.68x the one-token time. Less than 5x, because the weights are read once for all 5 tokens, but far from free: on this engine and weight format, 2 and 3 tokens use a kernel that handles each token almost separately, and only from 4 tokens does a small-batch kernel share the weight reads (the paragraph below). The derived H100 curve (a toggle on the chart below) stays within 10% of the one-token time up to about 165 tokens.

sd-pr2.text: Measured 1.84 tokens per step at k = 4 (mean of 3 seeds); the formula with α = 0.48 gives 1.89. Over all 72 combinations of prompt, temperature and k run here, the formula's median error was 3% and its largest 17%: close, once you know α.

drafters.setup: Target Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M (Qwen official GGUF, 2.50 GB) in llama-server (llama.cpp b11146, Metal, flash attention on), one slot, greedy, up to 512 tokens per answer, each prompt once (llama-server timings are per request; greedy output is deterministic). Prompts: a 70-line Python module to edit (add type hints; rename a function and change a constant), a WikiText-2 article to quote from and to summarise, a short story and a numbered list. Every drafter is the one published for Qwen3-4B (or the same-family 0.6B model), converted to GGUF here. measured here
drafters.note: One-minute load average before the runs: 5.5 to 76.1. The reference is the mean of three no-drafter runs (first, middle and last), which differed from their mean by up to 21% per prompt: speed-ups within that of 1x are noise.
drafters.findings:
• Code: add type hints: fastest n-gram simple, n 4, m 16 at 2.26x the plain server; longest acceptance 10.4 tokens per pass (DFlash, block 16 (k = 15)).
  • Code: rename: fastest n-gram simple, defaults (n 12, m 48) at 2.97x the plain server; longest acceptance 12.5 tokens per pass (DFlash, block 16 (k = 15)).
  • Quote from a passage: fastest n-gram simple, defaults (n 12, m 48) at 3.18x the plain server; longest acceptance 12.1 tokens per pass (DFlash, block 16 (k = 15)).
  • Summarise an article: fastest n-gram simple, n 4, m 16 at 1.05x the plain server; longest acceptance 3.5 tokens per pass (Qwen3-0.6B draft, k = 6).
  • Story: fastest n-gram simple, n 4, m 16 at 1.15x the plain server; longest acceptance 2.3 tokens per pass (DSpark, block 7 (k = 7)).
  • List: fastest DFlash, block 16 (k = 15) at 2.25x the plain server; longest acceptance 10.4 tokens per pass (DFlash, block 16 (k = 15)).

All runs are greedy, so drafted and accepted counts repeat exactly from run to run (checked on two drafters run twice), and in exact arithmetic the text would equal the plain server's. It did not always: answer lengths differed from the plain server's for summarise an article with some drafter, the same floating-point effect as in Reading section 3 (a k + 1 token verification pass rounds differently from a 1-token step).

What it means. Model-free n-gram drafting was the clear winner wherever the answer copies the prompt (code edits, quoting), because its guesses cost nothing to make and are long; on fresh prose it finds nothing to copy and costs almost nothing either. The trained drafters guessed far better on prose than any n-gram, and DFlash's block of 16 was accepted 10 to 12 tokens at a time on code and lists, which is the only place its one-pass draft paid. EAGLE-3 and DSpark kept their acceptance but lost speed: on this GPU every drafted token makes the 4-bit target's verification pass costlier (Reading section 1), and the drafters run in 16-bit. This ranking is for one laptop GPU at batch 1, and it is not the datacenter ranking: on an H100, where checking 8 to 16 tokens is nearly free, the published results in Reading section 6 put EAGLE-3 and DFlash far ahead of n-gram on general text.
